native_result.query: The effect of which variable on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 to 0.0923 (while becoming insignifcant) when both SES and academic characteristics are included in analysis?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.3636  (significant) to  -0.2293 (insignificant) and effect of race on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024  (significant) to 0.0923 (insignificant) when academic characteristics are considered.
native_result.HypoB: The effect of SES (socioeconomic status) on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 (base model, highly significant, OR≈1.6) to 0.0923 (statistically insignificant) when both SES and academic characteristics are included in the analysis: SES's association with degree completion is largely explained by academic characteristics (class rank percentile / ASVAB ability), so after controlling for them SES has little or no independent effect on BA completion.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (n=8773, 9 variables, 0 missing; BA completed in 236 cases, 2.69%). 2) Fit logistic (logit) regressions treating each of the 8 variables as the candidate: base model (candidate alone) vs full models (candidate + SES + academic characteristics; academics variants: ABILITY+PERCENTILE, ABILITY only, PERCENTILE only), in original and standardized scales. 3) Only SES reproduces the 0.5024 -> 0.0923 attenuation pattern (base b=0.4729, p=1e-08; full with class rank b=0.0814, p=0.372, insignificant). 4) Sensitivity: PERCENTILE as quartiles (b=0.1073, p=0.234), female subsample (0.4995 -> 0.1082, p=0.379), VIF checks (1.27-2.26). Conclusion: SES is the variable whose effect on BA completion is diluted to insignificance once SES and academic characteristics are in the model.
